title: Is there enough CD47 and HLA-E on the cells in the first hours?
plain: Two signals tell the immune system's natural killer cells and macrophages to leave the new cells alone. If the cells carry too little of either signal in the first hours, those attackers can destroy them before the other protections matter.
detail: In Design A (Arm 1B), an internal EEF1A1 promoter drives CD47 constitutively (238,004 molecules per cell computational prior; Stage-0 gate at least 200,000) and an internal 5xISRE promoter drives HLA-E (release gate at least 15,000 molecules per cell, while the proposed Design X signal aims for 25,000; 10,890 computational resting prior). Endogenous B2M read-through is not credited as productive HLA-E expression, and resting surface density on stage 7 beta cells and endothelial cells is unmeasured (rule GY-009).
settle: Count CD47 and HLA-E molecules on the surface of edited cells at hour zero with calibrated flow cytometry (the rule names QuantiBRITE beads), and compare with the target.

title: Does SERPINB9 really block the killer-cell toxin as designed?
plain: Killer immune cells fire a toxin called granzyme B into their targets. The design makes the cells carry SERPINB9, a protein that should block that toxin. A computer cannot tell us whether it works, so only a lab test can.
detail: The flexible loop of SERPINB9 that engages granzyme B cannot be modelled reliably by structure prediction, so whether the inserted protein blocks granzyme B at the needed level is unresolved.
settle: A lab test of whether cells carrying the SERPINB9 design survive exposure to granzyme B.

title: Can the patient's own immune cells restart the attack using debris from the graft?
plain: Cells with no HLA flags are hard for T cells to see directly. But the patient's own immune cells can pick up debris from the graft and show it to T cells, which can restart the attack that caused the diabetes.
detail: Donor B2M-/- and CIITA-/- block direct presentation but not indirect presentation of shed secretome and debris by host dendritic cells on HLA-DQ2/DQ8 (rule GY-010). The design responds with small clusters, pre-built vessels and protection that switches on with inflammation, but this is not yet measured.
settle: Mix the patient's immune cells with debris from flag-free islets, and look for T-cell activation and cell damage.
source: Concise specification sections 4.2 and 9; rule GY-010

title: Does one kept HLA-C gene calm natural killer cells enough?
plain: Design B keeps one matched HLA-C gene so that natural killer cells see the cells as the patient's own. It is not yet known whether a single copy gives enough of that calming signal.
detail: After HLA-A and HLA-B deletion, a single retained HLA-C allele must supply enough leader peptide to stabilise surface HLA-E (rule GY-005). It also requires choosing the right HLA-C haplotype.
settle: Measure surface HLA-E and natural killer cell response in cells that keep a single HLA-C allele after HLA-A and HLA-B are switched off.
source: Concise specification sections 4.5 and 9; rule GY-005

title: Does the oxygen supply hold up under pessimistic assumptions?
plain: A new graft has no blood vessels at first, so it carries its own oxygen for the first three days. In the computer model the margin inside each cluster of cells is thin, and the model uses a single 68-hour oxygen-release half-life across recipes that pack more calcium peroxide into smaller beads. With a faster or slower release, or late blood vessels, oxygen or peroxide safety can fail.
detail: In the 14-day model the homogenized slab average minimum is 19.9 mmHg, while the two-zone cluster model gives a conservative gel-only core oxygen of 2.15 mmHg (0.15 mmHg above the 2.0 mmHg core-necrosis floor; uniform-supply is 4.08 mmHg and homogenized Dirichlet is 8.64 mmHg), alongside an unrounded joint grid of late-connecting and weaker blood vessels and a zero-vessel lower bound (IIP-0002). Twenty of the 21 main PDE regimes also carry over a single unvalidated 68.0-hour oxygen-release half-life from a 25 wt% (10.55 vol%) monolithic silicone disk (Pedraza 2012, PMID 22371586) to 31.25 wt% (13.86 vol%, Layout B) and 46.39 wt% (23.45 vol%, Stage-0 Design X) microbeads with surface-immobilised catalase (IIP-0010). Across an 84-regime fixed-inventory sweep, Stage-0 Design X passes only from 34 to 87 hours at a 36-hour vascular midpoint under first-order or reaction shrinking-core release, narrows to 34 to 68 hours at a 60-hour midpoint, and has no passing half-life when Ginstling-Brounshtein diffusion kinetics combine with a 60-hour midpoint.
settle: Measure crystal and microbead size distributions, oxygen-release half-life and kinetic law for each calcium-peroxide recipe in its implanted form, and measure oxygen inside real graft slabs over the first 3 days across delayed or weak vascular ingrowth.
source: Concise specification sections 5 and 9; IIP-0002 and IIP-0010

title: Do many gene edits at once cause DNA rearrangements?
plain: Each extra edit is another chance for the cell's DNA to be rearranged by mistake, and cells with cancer-linked changes could take over. This is why the scoring model penalises extra edits.
detail: Adenine base editors caused DNA rearrangements in the cited study (PMID 39529170). The project extends that concern to multiple base and prime edits as an engineering precaution (rule GY-006). Manufacturing would need deep sequencing checks for cancer-linked changes.
settle: Deep sequencing of edited cell lines for rearrangements and cancer-linked changes, with the same checks repeated at manufacturing scale.
source: Concise specification sections 4.5 and 9; rule GY-006

title: Which starting assumptions drive the scores?
plain: The scores are estimates, not predictions. Almost all of the difference between designs comes from the team's starting assumptions and very little from published findings. Lab results will replace the assumptions one at a time.
detail: {{assumptions}} per cent of the spread in scores across the {{designs}} designs comes from starting assumptions, {{overlap}} per cent from the overlap of assumptions and findings, and {{findingsShare}} per cent from published findings.
settle: Replace each assumption with a measurement as lab results arrive, starting with the ones that move the scores most.

title: Which form of CD47 is best: the full-length protein or a surface-anchored form?
plain: CD47 tells macrophages not to eat the cell. The full-length version also sends signals inside the cell that can blunt insulin release. A shorter, surface-anchored version leaves out the inside signals and keeps the macrophage signal. Whether insulin release is spared is not yet tested, so the two are being compared.
detail: Full-length CD47 can blunt glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Ghimire 2023, PMID 37820008) and block new blood vessels. An IgV-GPI form kept the macrophage signal without cell death or blocked blood-vessel growth in non-islet immune, blood-stem-cell and endothelial models (Jurkat, A20, mouse LSK cells and EA.hy926 endothelial plugs; Xu 2024, PMID 38508139, Tier 2B), while the 180,000 to 220,000 molecules-per-cell protection transition in Hu 2023 (PMID 37156915) comes from virus-titrated primary human islets measured with clone CC2C6 and Quantibrite beads (engineered HIP cells reached over 600,000; IIP-0008). Insulin release and macrophage protection with IgV-GPI in stem-cell islets remain untested.
settle: Compare insulin release and macrophage protection side by side for each CD47 form in stem-cell islets, cross-calibrating clone B6H12 and clone CC2C6 Quantibrite surface counts.

title: Which layout should be used to add CD47 and HLA-E at B2M?
plain: Two ways of adding the two genes are being compared. One reads them as a single unit and is too long for the usual delivery virus. The other gives each gene its own switch and fits.
detail: Layout 1 joins the genes with a 2A sequence (4,880 base pairs, over the single-AAV6 limit, so non-viral delivery would be needed). Layout 2 uses two promoters facing opposite directions with no 2A joint (3,974 base pairs, fits one AAV6 virus).
settle: Build both layouts and compare expression level, editing yield and delivery.

title: At CXCL10, does it matter which protective gene comes first?
plain: The design adds two protective genes at one spot, SERPINB9 and PD-L1, so they switch on only when inflammation appears. The current order is SERPINB9 first. A lab test would compare it with the reverse order.
detail: Locus 3 is CXCL10::SERPINB9-GSG-P2A-PD-L1. It is compared with CXCL10::PD-L1-GSG-P2A-SERPINB9 in a planned decision experiment.
settle: Edit cells with each order and compare survival under inflammation and killer-cell attack.

title: Does a sequence in Design B's CXCL10 edit act as an unintended switch?
plain: Design B drops one linking sequence at the CXCL10 spot to avoid leaving a piece that the kept HLA-C gene could show to T cells as foreign. In exchange, a piece of the design might switch genes on at the wrong time. That has to be ruled out.
detail: Design B uses a 2A-free layout at the CXCL10 locus. An internal promoter or eIF4G leader sequence can have cryptic promoter activity (PMID 12370285).
settle: Test whether the sequence drives expression on its own, outside inflammation.

title: Can the safety switch remove almost every cell?
plain: Every cell carries a safety switch that a drug (AP1903) should trigger to remove them. The proposed target is fewer than one cell in 100 million able to regrow. Nothing has shown that yet.
detail: iCasp9 is inserted on both AAVS1 copies from a promoter active in every cell type, flanked by an HNRNPA2B1-proximal 455 bp CpG-core anti-silencing candidate (GRCh38 chr7:26200580-26201034; CBX3 is a legacy alias, not proof of identity to the published CBX3-side fragment). Stage-0 tests compare four anti-silencing and orientation arms alongside matched 2x2 co-directional and convergent splice-cleaned comparators (Knight 2012, PMID 22696657; excluding intron-blocking SPA poly(A) inside PPP1R12C) while checking host-gene (PPP1R12C) splicing, calibrated minigene and clonal UMI junction sequencing (at least 3,700 UMIs), double-stranded RNA stress and DNA methylation alongside the untouched reference donor, and audit local geometry across three crystal structures of the switch's domains (PDB 1BL4, 1JXQ and 1NW9; IIP-0011 and IIP-0015). The bound of one in 100 million counts only cells able to regrow, which is a different endpoint from the early bulk-kill screen (99.9% of cells killed). Killing efficiency in hypoxic, immature or rogue cells across all 9.335 x 10^8 total living cells (including endothelial and pericyte support cells) is unmeasured (rule GY-002 excludes lineage-restricted switches).
settle: Compare the AAVS1 anti-silencing, orientation and splice-cleaned arms across maturation with calibrated minigene and UMI junction sequencing, check PPP1R12C splicing, double-stranded RNA stress and CpG methylation, and give AP1903 to edited cultures, including at low oxygen, to count clonogenic survivors.
source: Concise specification sections 4.4 and 9; IIP-0011 and IIP-0015

title: Is switching off TYK2 worth its cost in insulin-making cells?
plain: In the model, switching off TYK2 helps against rejection, autoimmune attack and early attack. But it costs about a third of the insulin-making cells while they grow. Whether the trade is worth it in the full design is not known.
detail: Design B switches off TYK2. Chandra 2022 (PMID 36289205) reports about 32 per cent fewer insulin-making cells during differentiation.
settle: Measure insulin-making cell yield and immune protection in the full Design B, with and without the TYK2 edit.

title: X is two different candidates, not one verified product
plain: The name Design X covers two separate things: a scored comparison on the 2,160-design grid (Design A plus one insulin-gene base edit, using the baseline 119 micrometre oxygen layer) and an unscored Stage-0 upgrade proposal (new B2M switch and CD47 variant, a protective insulin-gene cell line, an outer-ring Fas-ligand gel layout and a 100 micrometre oxygen layer, with no insulin-gene edit). Neither is built or tested.
detail: Clarified in IIP-0009. The scored grid candidate (ISLET1_CHASSIS_X_EMERGENT_CHALLENGER, K=4, B=1) adds an INS base edit to Design A on the baseline 119 micrometre Layout B oxygen layer and is tied for second place on the grid. The separate Stage-0 molecular and pouch proposal (K=4, B=0) changes the B2M promoter and CD47 sequence, selects an INS-VNTR Class III starting line, arranges SA-FasL microgels in an outer boundary ring around a 100 micrometre central oxygen layer, and has no score or built DNA.
settle: Keep separate identities, provide the exact donor and protein ledger, and qualify each product before any promotion.

title: Does the proposed outer-band pouch physically fit?
plain: In the baseline geometry used for the scores across Designs A, B and X, a 350 micrometre slab with a 119 micrometre central oxygen layer leaves two outer bands of 115.5 micrometres, slightly narrower than 120 micrometre cell clusters. The Stage-0 versions of Design A and Design X thin the central layer to 100 micrometres, leaving 125 micrometre outer bands and capping clusters at 100 micrometres so they fit on paper. Nothing has been built or measured yet.
detail: Clarified in IIP-0009. Changing source-lamina porosity while holding oxygen inventory fixed is a conditional sensitivity, not a scored design input. In the scored Layout B baseline shared by the grid rows for Designs A, B and X, a 350 micrometre slab with a 34% central lamina (119 micrometres) leaves two 115.5 micrometre outer bands, too narrow to contain 120 micrometre spheres without compression. Stage-0 Embodiment A* and Stage-0 Design X thin the central lamina to 100 micrometres (125 micrometre outer bands, clusters at most 100 micrometres), which fits on paper but raises solid CaO2 loading to 46.39 wt% (23.45 vol%) and remains unbuilt.
settle: Reconcile local cell packing, bead inventory, source geometry and cluster dimensions in one physical design before claiming an oxygen improvement.

title: Which assumptions and definition of success sit behind the four-hurdle odds estimate?
plain: The 21% and 37% figures are rough judgements for clearing four in-body hurdles in sequence, assuming the edited cells work as designed and pass lab safety checks before any trial. Moving from one design to three depends on how much the designs overlap at each hurdle, and the estimate depends on which clinical outcome counts as success.
detail: Raised in IIP-0003 (issue #3). Each step in the four-hurdle estimate is judged for a design still in the running after the earlier hurdles, and the three-design figure depends on how strongly Designs A, B and X share failure modes at each hurdle. Lab release gates (OQ-012 safety-switch escape, OQ-006 DNA rearrangements, and product-specific Gate 1 insulin and glucagon function) sit outside the four hurdles as pre-trial pass/fail conditions, and a single clinical endpoint (such as one-year insulin independence without anti-rejection drugs and without severe hypoglycaemia) must be fixed before replacing starting judgements with data.
settle: Fix one clinical definition of success, write down the per-design and shared failure assumptions at each hurdle, and replace the starting judgements with measured pass rates as lab and preclinical results arrive.

title: Can a Stage-1 multi-lineage immune–islet co-culture catch cross-talk missed by split assays without hiding which edit failed?
plain: Stage 0 tests T cells, natural killer cell subsets and macrophages in separate wells so each gene edit gets a clear pass or fail. In the body those immune cells act together and amplify one another's signals. A combined human immune–islet test in Stage 1 might catch failure modes that split tests miss, provided background donor mismatch and gel recovery do not blur the readout.
detail: Raised in IIP-0007 (issue #7). Stage-0 Readouts 3A, 3B and 3C stay separate and mandatory for clean per-edit attribution. Before adding a supplementary combined human PBMC, antigen-presenting-cell, natural-killer and macrophage co-culture with microgel-embedded stem-cell islets in Stage 1, three technical checks have to pass: separating non-specific donor mismatch from autoimmune attack over 48 to 72 hours, keeping every immune cell type alive in islet medium without artificial cytokine-activated killer effects, and recovering intact clusters from the gel to measure glucose-triggered insulin and glucagon release afterwards (comparing modular human immune co-cultures in Higbee 2009 PMID 19807200, Byers 2009 PMID 19272794 and Ma 2010 PMID 20331478 with autologous stem-cell-islet immune co-culture in Leite 2020 PMID 32668238).
settle: Keep Stage-0 Readouts 3A, 3B and 3C separate, then run a Stage-1 qualification pilot testing 48 to 72 hour background lysis, multi-lineage survival without artificial cytokine activation, and post-challenge insulin secretion recovery.

title: Do insulin and glucagon release recover after low oxygen, and can higher-beta mixes match the 60:30:10 default?
plain: Surviving the first 14 days of low oxygen does not guarantee that the cells still release insulin and glucagon properly afterwards. Separately, packing more beta cells into each cluster could shrink the graft if insulin shut-off and low-sugar glucagon rescue still hold up.
detail: Raised in IIP-0004 and IIP-0006. Surviving a 336-hour hypoxic bridge does not establish preserved glucose-regulated insulin secretion, rapid shut-off, or low-glucose glucagon rescue during and after reoxygenation (Wang 2025, PMID 40404627; Chendke 2023, PMID 37476069). Stage 0 measures hormone function after recovery before crediting functional dose, and compares intermediate beta:alpha:delta mixtures (70:20:10, 70:25:5, 80:15:5 and 80:10:10) beside the 60:30:10 default and pure beta-cell controls (Perez-Frances 2024, PMID 39169271), keeping 60:30:10 unless independent batches pass both shut-off and glucagon-rescue checks.
settle: Measure dynamic insulin secretion, 3-minute shut-off and low-sugar glucagon release after recovery from the 14-day low-oxygen window, and compare intermediate beta:alpha:delta mixtures against 60:30:10 across independent differentiation batches.
source: Concise specification sections 5 and 9; IIP-0004 and IIP-0006

title: Do the core gene insertions leave nearby genes and splicing intact, and does shed PD-L1 act in the liquid around the graft?
plain: Inserting protective genes at B2M, CXCL10 and AAVS1 or switching off CIITA could accidentally disturb nearby genes, splice in either direction into surrounding host exons, form repeated hairpins in AAV6 templates, or lose promoter activity over time. At CXCL10, enzymes can also clip PD-L1 off the cell surface into the surrounding liquid, where its effect on immune cells is unknown.
detail: Raised in IIP-0005, IIP-0011 and IIP-0015. Sequence, two-strand splice-motif and repeat scans flag places to test (and reconcile the 326 Class-I and 112 Class-II boundary peptide windows across the reference junctions) without certifying splicing safety, while all canonical reference FASTAs remain untouched. Stage 0 tracks Arm 1B promoter CpG methylation and tests a silent HLA-E stop-seam comparator at B2M against splicing into B2M exon 2 (32-amino-acid foreign tail), checks CIITA transcript clean-up, verifies at CXCL10 (4q21.1) that CXCL9, CXCL11 and opposite-strand ART3 stay undisturbed while comparing one-factor-at-a-time synonymous PD-L1 variants (Forrest 2020, PMID 32053646), a bGH 3'-end cleavage check and an optional single-sided 80 bp cHS4 FII element avoiding AAV6 hairpin repeats (Xie 2017, PMID 28462820), runs calibrated EndoC-betaH1 minigene and clonal UMI junction sequencing (at least 3,700 UMIs) across Loci 1, 3 and 4, and tests minimally processed cell-free medium conditioned by inflamed edited islets on an independent PD-1 reporter beside protease-shedding assays (Hira-Miyazawa 2018, PMID 29345283).
settle: Run calibrated host-context minigene assays, clonal UMI splice-junction sequencing (at least 3,700 UMIs), host-mRNA equivalence checks and bisulfite methylation assays across resting and inflamed edited islets alongside the one-factor-at-a-time Stage-0 comparators, and test cell-free conditioned medium with and without PD-L1 blockade on a stimulated PD-1 reporter.
source: Concise specification sections 4.1 to 4.4, 6 and 9; IIP-0005, IIP-0011 and IIP-0015

title: Do edited islets stay protected after temporary gel signals wear off, and can added CD55 help without hurting insulin release?
plain: Temporary gel particles carrying clotting-control and Fas-ligand proteins wash out after the early transplant window, which could let the immune system rebound against the bare cells. Adding a extra complement shield (CD55) must also be tested on the exact same edited cells while keeping the cell's own CD59 insulin-release machinery intact.
detail: Raised in IIP-0012. Prior SA-FasL microgel studies used short-course rapamycin and measured fluorescent retention rather than functional depletion half-life (Headen 2018, PMID 29867165; Lei 2022, PMID 35559682; Turan 2024, PMID 38709159). Stage 0 compares never-conditioned, conditioned-then-depleted and active-gel sibling aliquots under fresh complement and T-cell rechallenge, tests ectopic CD55(SCR1-4) on the identical edited background while preserving endogenous intracellular CD59 isoforms needed for insulin exocytosis (Golec 2022, PMID 35666870; van der Torren 2017, PMID 27787618), and holds four extra candidate edits (TYMS, NLRC5, endogenous CD274 activation and TXNIP) outside core designs behind pre-registered pass gates.
settle: Compare never-treated, gel-depleted and active-gel edited islets under fresh human serum and T-cell rechallenge, and test edited islets with and without ectopic CD55 for complement survival and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
